title: Children linked to religious sect raided by UK police now subject of care proceedings
summary:
Scale of cases in family court relating to Ahmadi Religion of Peace and Light ‘rarely seen before’, one lawyer said

Scores of children linked to a religious sect raided by police over…

blocks.text: Scores of children linked to a religious sect raided by police over allegations of serious sexual offences and modern slavery are now the subject of care proceedings, court documents have revealed.

Family courts are dealing with more than 40 cases in relation to “a very significant number of children” who were living at the compound run by the Ahmadi Religion of Peace and Light (AROPL), when it was raided by police in April.
The findings can be reported after the courts overturned requests from AROPL members to stop the judgment being published.
The sheer scale of the cases coming through the family courts has “rarely been seen before”, a family lawyer has said, representing almost one in 20 care cases at the family court in Manchester.

More than 100 people were living at Webb House, a former orphanage in Crewe in north-west England and AROPL’s headquarters. The sect blends tenets of Islam with conspiracy theories about the Illuminati and aliens controlling US presidents.

blocks.caption: Fourteen people have been arrested on suspicion of offences including human trafficking, sexual assault, rape, forced marriage and modern day slavery. One has since been released.  Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

blocks.text: Police have since arrested 14 people on suspicion of offences including human trafficking, sexual assault, rape, forced marriage and modern day slavery. One suspect has been released with no further action.

Cheshire constabulary has been at pains to explain that it is investigating individual people and not the sect as a whole. But the force said the raid raised concerns in relation to the welfare of children who were members of the group.
A judgment from Mr Justice Hayden in the Manchester family court published on Tuesday in the case of two of the children laid out a series of concerns from police and social services.

Representatives from the local authority told the court that conditions in the dormitories where children are reported to have lived were “observed to be neglectful with dirty bedding”. CCTV cameras were found inside the children’s dormitories.
Concerns were also raised about the educational provision for the children in the group. The court heard that most of the children were home schooled via computer screens.
Knives were recovered during the police raid on the property along with a sharps bin, suggesting injections may have been administered outside of a registered medical setting.

The ruling, which was handed down in June but published only on Tuesday, dismissed one parent’s attempt to appeal against the interim order granted by a judge. Interim orders are issued during care proceedings. They grant the local authority, in this case Cheshire East council, shared parental responsibility for the children.
The mother argued that she was choosing to remain with the group and felt that the court order meant she was “being dictated how I am to live my life and who is able to live with me”.
Hayden found there was no legitimate reason to dismiss the orders while the family court cases played out, a process that may take months.

The majority of children from AROPL who are now under interim care orders have remained with their families while they wait for the court to explore their cases. None of them are still living at the group’s headquarters.

Alex O’Dwyer Curran, a family lawyer from Payne Hicks Beach who is not involved in the proceedings, said there was “little doubt about the sheer scale of this litigation”, adding that “it is difficult to identify a comparable case in the history of the modern family court”.

blocks.caption: None of the children who are under interim care orders are still living at the group’s headquarters. Photograph: AROPL

blocks.text: Lawyers for the families involved sought to prevent publication of details relating to the care orders of the children. They argued publication of the judgment would put “significant new information into the public domain” and could “reheat the hostility to the community, and risk exposing children and parents to physical and emotional harm and potential public disorder”.
Media organisations, including the Guardian and Press Association, resisted the attempt to stop the judgment being published.
In his rejection of the application, Hayden wrote: “The court cannot simply close its doors in response to unspecified concerns about potential civil disorder.”
The Guardian has previously reported that former residents of the site had expressed concerns about the wellbeing and education of the children there.

Cheshire East council’s social services have twice made inquiries relating to the group or the children in the past. There is no evidence to suggest that action was deemed necessary on those occasions.

Two relatives of a teenager living at the Crewe premises have previously told the Guardian that the teenager told them he was unhappy living with the group and wanted to leave. His family members said they were concerned that he was not in formal education but was being home-schooled at the site.

AROPL’s lawyer said at the time that the organisation was not involved in home schooling, which was led by parents. The group had considered setting up a formal school, the lawyer said, but had shelved the idea and dismantled classrooms inside Webb House.
AROPL followers are warned about the corrupting influence of mainstream education on children and are encouraged to “take advantage of laws” in countries that enable home schooling.
